in_context.text: This is the elder's greeting at the start of a short letter. He wishes grace, mercy and peace from both the Father and Jesus Christ, "in truth and love." Those two words, truth and love, run through the whole letter that follows.

speaker.text: "The elder," who does not give his name. Early Christian tradition identifies him as John the apostle. Some scholars think he was a different church leader.

audience.text: "The elect lady and her children." This may be a Christian woman and her family, or a figurative name for a local church and its members. The letter does not say which.

what.text: A blessing names three gifts: grace, mercy and peace. Their source is God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, "the Son of the Father." They come "in truth and love." Paul opens 1 Timothy with the same three gifts from the same two givers.

events.text: The greeting opens the letter. The text itself gives no date.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 85-95, late in John's life, near the time of 1 John. Scholarly view: most scholars also place it in the late first century.

where.text: The letter does not say where it was written or sent. Early tradition places John's last years in Ephesus. The readers were a church or household he hoped to visit, likely in the province of Asia.

purpose.text: The greeting sets up the letter's two concerns. The readers are to walk in truth and love, and they are to refuse deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

big_picture.text: The verse calls Jesus "the Son of the Father." Later in the letter, whoever abides in the doctrine of Christ "hath both the Father and the Son." 1 John 2:23 says the same: denying the Son means not having the Father.

for_readers.text: God's gifts come joined to truth and love, not to one without the other. Other letters also link faith and love "which is in Christ Jesus."

why_it_matters.text: The lexicon gives this form as "will be," from the verb "to be." This fits verse 2, where the truth "shall be with us for ever."
It means mercy, pity or compassion. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly translates the Hebrew word chesed. The same word appears in Paul's greeting to Timothy.
In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly translates shalom. It is used for agreement and harmony between people, not just the absence of war.

It can mean true teaching, especially Christian doctrine, or truthfulness and integrity of character. The letter uses both senses. The truth "dwelleth in us," and believers are found "walking in truth."
The word covers people's love for one another and God's love for people. The letter defines it as walking after God's commandments. 1 John 4:10 roots it in God sending his Son.

takeaway.text: Grace, mercy and peace come from the Father and the Son together. They come "in truth and love," the two things this letter will not let anyone separate.

resolved.reason: The lexicon only says the word chiefly translates חֶסֶד in the Greek Old Testament. It does not define that Hebrew word as 'God's steadfast kindness', and its own example (Gen 21:23) uses it of human kindness.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
